title: Chapter 9 — Before Something Changes
text:
The <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> job had ended at 21:47 by the overlay clock. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> rode back the way he always did. He'd spent just under an hour folded into a drawer at <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> — concealment work, waiting out a courier who never knew he was there. His hands had found the bag seam in the dark before his eyes caught up.

At 20:54 the concealment door had opened four seconds early. Not much. Four seconds fell inside casual variance, the kind of gap that never makes a report. His neuretics made a different call: TIMING VARIANCE — EXTERNAL — SOURCE UNCLASSIFIED. The courier had come through 53 seconds ahead of his window. Nothing explained the early open. No one on the personnel log. No environmental trigger on record. The door had simply been open when it needed to be, on a track keyed to a five-minute intake cycle it wasn't supposed to break, then sealed itself back onto that cycle as if it had never moved.

He'd been in the work long enough to tell the two apart — a door someone opens, and a door that opens because something else decided it should. He'd started the counter the moment the notation hit the job log. He hadn't decided yet what to do with it.

He didn't remember deciding to come here.

The door was unlocked. It usually was when she worked, which was most of the time, so he pushed it open and went in. It whispered shut on its pneumatic seal behind him. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was at the bench under the ceiling light, her hair in an updo that had been precise three hours ago and was loosening now. She didn't look up from the sensor array she was calibrating. She never looked up on entry. She knew the sound of his step on the stair before the door frame finished moving.

"Calibration's running," she said.

Not an invitation. Not a refusal. Information, flat, the way she offered everything.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the door another beat. The room was warm. The bench light threw a clean cone over her hands, the array, the tools laid out in the order she always used. Through the cracked window the wet street eleven floors down smelled like factory rain drying off ferrocement — pear drops and machine oil, and under it the lake-cold that lived in the air here no matter the month. On the secondary bench, the arm she was building for Oziel lay half-assembled in its jig: a full prosthetic, articulated, the motor tendons still loose. Friday work.

He took off the jacket and set <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> against the wall in the usual spot, the near corner by the secondary bench, out of the way. She'd known it was there the first time he set it down without asking, and she hadn't said anything then either.

He sat on the stool. The stool wasn't his. She'd never told him to use it. Nothing lived on it — no tools, no parts, no reason to keep it clear except that she did. He used it anyway, the way he always did now.

In the lower-left of his overlay, the counter ran. 56:41. 56:42. He rested his right hand on his knee, the chemical-burn scar on the palm turned up to the light.

He tried to pull the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> door log again, quietly, while she worked — a second look, cross-referenced against the building's environmental grid. It came back the way it had come back four times already: access-restricted past the surface layer, the deeper timestamps walled behind a permission set his neuretics couldn't touch. What surfaced instead was a clean lie — 0545 to 0550, SCHEDULED CYCLE — no deviation, no early open, no timestamp for the thing he'd watched happen with his own eyes. He pushed at it anyway, ran the query through the back channel he kept for jobs like this. AUTHENTICATION REFUSED. Then, a half-second later, something he hadn't asked for: a flag on his own query. Somewhere, a system had noticed him looking, and logged the fact. The counter didn't stop. It couldn't. Whatever had opened that door was reading his interest in it as clearly as he was reading the door — and he had just told it he was still counting.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands moved over the array with the unhurried precision three years of fieldwork had built into them — steadier than training or drugs could account for, earned one job at a time, nobody's gift but her own. The work had a rhythm. A tool lifted, set, adjusted. A small current run through the rebuilt joints, a reading taken off the handheld scope, marked in shorthand precise and economical, without pause.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s boots sat on the floor. He held the fact of the door in his chest and said nothing about it. She didn't ask. She never asked — some problems wanted presence, not words, and both of them had learned that without agreeing to it out loud.

He had no reason to be here. He stayed.

The calibration moved through its intervals. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat on the stool and watched the bench without watching <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>, and after a while he wasn't watching any of it — just the light, the tools, the feel of the quiet. It wasn't the quiet of an empty room.

She set a probe down, made a note on the small slate she kept for calibration records, and picked the probe back up. She worked the next interval. Her hands moved with the unhurried precision the work had built into them — a tool lifted, set, adjusted, a reading taken and marked. The scar tissue on her left palm caught the light, old work, older than the three years they'd been doing this. He'd never asked how she got it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> got off the stool. He wanted to see the marker on the near edge — to read what she'd written there and know how close the array had come to naming the thing at the carousel. The slate never synced to anything. Paper the same. She kept the numbers that mattered off the network, in a hand no scanner could pull, and he'd learned to read her notation the way you learn a language by living inside it — no instruction, just attention paid across enough repetitions that the symbols resolved into meaning.

He didn't have a reason for that either. The stool was at the secondary bench and the array was at the primary bench, and his feet carried him across the floor with the same economy they carried him through everything. He stopped. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s arm was to his right. The array sat between them. Her elbow rode the edge of the surface, angled toward the part she was checking, and the gap between his arm and hers was small.

She didn't move. She kept working, the probe tracing the path it had to trace. She wasn't pretending he wasn't there. She was just going on, and his being there changed nothing about the calibration.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the array. It was a three-axis unit, civilian grade — the kind used to monitor the air in closed spaces. Low end of the spectrum, down where buildings and machines hum without meaning to. Seventeen to nineteen hertz, if you stood in the right place. Three weeks ago she'd written the carousel cross-streets in the margin of these notes, in the small tidy hand she used for things she meant to find again. She'd been building the array ever since — an instrument tuned to the exact band his neuretics kept flagging as AMBIENT INTERFERENCE, TYPE UNCLASSIFIED. He'd never asked what it was for. He knew. His own hardware couldn't name the thing at the carousel. She was building something that could. He'd said one piece of it out loud, once, and she'd started making a way to see the rest.

He reached toward the marker at the near edge — the same reflex that had found the bag seam in the dark at <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity>. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s probe came down across his line of reach. Not touching him. Just in the way. A thin line of resistance between his hand and the paper, a wordless no written in her own still hand. He drew back.

"That one running hot?" he asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> glanced at it. "It's within spec. The humidity's skewing the read."

She didn't look up. Her eyes stayed on the readings, the steady drift of numbers that meant the calibration was still running, still listening, still learning the shape of the city's invisible noise.

The quiet came back. It wasn't hostile. That was the harder thing.

The calibration reached the parts-drawer stage. It came in every run she did — a point where a component needed swapping, and the spares lived in the drawer at the far end of the bench. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had watched it enough times to know the order. Probe down. Drawer open. Component chosen. Drawer shut. Probe up.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> reached past him.

Her arm crossed in front of his. The drawer was at the far end, past where he stood, and to reach it she had to stretch past him — and she did, steady and unhurried. She didn't ask him to move. She didn't pull back from how close it put them, and she didn't lean in either. She just reached, the way you reach across a bench for a thing you need, her arm passing within an inch of his chest. He felt the displacement of air, the warmth of it, the small specific weight of her occupying the space he occupied.

The drawer slid open with the soft precision of something she'd maintained herself — no stick, no catch, just the runners taking the weight. She found the component she wanted and turned it once in the light to read the spec marking before she drew back. Then she reached again and pushed the drawer shut.

The latch caught.

It was a small sound — the click of a well-kept drawer finding its seat. He'd heard it a hundred times in this room. Clean and final. The sound of a thing where it belonged.

Neither of them moved.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened his mouth. One sound came up — not a word. A half-syllable that started in the throat and stopped before it got out, before it found the shape that would have made it into anything. The sound of someone about to ask something and swallowing it whole.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands went still on the bench.

She'd heard it. She wasn't looking at him. Her hands lay flat, the probe held level between her fingers, and she was still — not the stillness of someone who missed it, but of someone who caught it and was holding quiet on purpose. She was reading him the way she read a system, not with her eyes but with the part of her that registered when something changed state. Between that stillness and a word was a single breath. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the wall behind her. His overlay read 59:38. 59:39.

1:00:00.

He watched the counter roll over.

Then he closed it — the command running through his neuretics quiet and automatic, the kind of thing a body does when the mind is somewhere else. The lower-left of his overlay went blank.

On the secondary bench, Oziel's arm sat in its jig, the motor tendons loose and waiting.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said her name.

She looked up from the array.

"I'll be in the armory if you need a second set of hands."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s hands lifted off the bench. She picked up the probe. Tonight she meant to close the 17-to-19 band for good — pin the baseline down to a hard number, prove there was nothing living in it, and have the whole array signed off before the shift rolled over.

"I won't need one," she said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved toward the door. He didn't reach for the jacket first. He crossed to the near corner where <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> leaned against the wall. The saya was matte-black composite, friction-fitted, and the tsukaito cord was worn smooth at the grip points. He lifted it by the sheath, and the weight settled into the same grip it always found — not heavy, precise, the grip that knew where his fingers went. Then he took the jacket off the hook and put it on. The whole sequence took eight seconds. He didn't hurry any of it.

At the door he stopped. His hand found the frame. Not the latch, not the handle — just the edge where the door sat in the wall. He stood there a moment, the pneumatic seal a few inches from his palm, the bench light behind him and the hallway ahead. He didn't turn around.

He left.

The door closed on its seal, a small exhale of pressed air. The mechanism did exactly what it was built to do. No ceremony, no weight. The same sound it made every time.

In 2E, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> picked up the tool she'd set down. The calibration was where she'd left it, the markers still running, the probe still warm. She looked at the array. The 17-to-19 band read clean — baseline, no source, the same as every night since she'd built the thing. Whatever sat at 18.7 hertz at the carousel wasn't here tonight. That was either reassuring or the wrong question to ask.

She went back into the work.

On one side of her, the bench had six inches of empty space where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had been standing.

She didn't move to fill it.

title: Arrival
text:
He didn't go to the armory.

He told himself he would — the cool, low-lit room off the stairwell where the gear lived, where running a maintenance check was mechanical work that took just enough of his attention to keep the rest of him out of 2E all night, waiting on something that wasn't coming.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went to his apartment instead. He didn't turn on the light. The city glow came through the window in bars, enough to see the table and the terminal that sat waiting, and he pulled the chair out and sat with the overlay open in his left eye.

Three data points.

The first: an AMBIENT INTERFERENCE notation at the carousel park. 18.7 hertz, TYPE UNCLASSIFIED. Three weeks ago. He'd told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> about it, and she'd written the cross-streets in the margin of her notes. He pulled the raw log now. The spike lasted four minutes, then stopped — not a fade, not a drift into noise, a clean cutoff, a switch turning off.

The second: a TIMING VARIANCE notation at <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity>. EXTERNAL, SOURCE UNCLASSIFIED. The concealment door, four seconds early. Tonight. He held both points in the overlay, the carousel spike and the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> variance, and something in the geometry of them wanted to align. Not yet. Not cleanly. But the shape was there.

The third: <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s array, tuned to the 17-to-19 band, reading clean. He pulled her calibration data — the intervals she'd run since the carousel, an instrument built for exactly this band. Baseline every time. A tool made to see something that had stopped appearing.

He mapped them. The carousel park sat in West Town West, a mile and a half south. <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> was three miles north. His apartment sat between them, a block east. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s lab was thirty feet across the hall.

The source-unclassified tag showed on both the carousel notation and the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> one. Different neighborhoods. Different jobs. Three weeks apart. Both logged as external, neither with any mechanism or origin the system could name — his neuretics kept reaching for a classification and coming back with the same empty field.

And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s array — built for exactly this band after the carousel — had read clean tonight. That meant the source wasn't in 2E. Or it wasn't broadcasting tonight. Or it was something a fixed-point instrument would miss if it moved.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the three points for a long time. Absence, in the right geometry, was its own kind of presence. Not a line. Not a circle. Something that moved through the city and looked random until you saw all three pieces at once.

He opened the relay. The routing shell was thirty-two characters. He'd stared at that string long enough that it had stopped looking like anything. He didn't type a message. He didn't ask the question. He wasn't sure yet what the question was — which wasn't the same as not being ready to ask it, but only barely.

He closed the relay.

title: The Workbench
text:
He pulled the shell's registration history.

It was public record. Any freelancer could look up the operating certificate on a routing intermediary. Most never did. The certificate rendered in clean lines across the overlay: a West Loop address, a management entity called Clearlight Operations LLC, a registration date in 2209—six years before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> first worked with the shell.

Clearlight had filed five years of compliance reports, then stopped. Its address traced to a commercial mail service that had closed in 2210. The shell kept running without it. It routed contracts, cleared payments, held active certification with the <entity repo="place" guid="6a5b2384-072c-f6a9-b228-107570089917">Chicago</entity> Freelancer Registry. No human officer was listed anywhere.

He got up, drew a glass of water, and stood at the window. The synthesis corridor ran its 0100 shift—a maintenance crew working <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-728a-a754-075f608dd73a">the south side</entity>, the foot traffic thin, the particular quiet of people who kept this hour. He finished the water and went back to the terminal.

The CFR required a human officer of record. The shell had one: a name <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't know, a credential number that checked out, an address that turned out to be a second mail service, also closed. He searched the name. A valid credential. A freelance operations license. Nothing else in any system he could reach. No social address. No transaction history. A credential that existed, attached to a person who—as far as the record knew—had never once touched it. A name with the weight of a real thing and the texture of something built to be forgotten.

He went further back. He'd come to the shell in 2215, through a contact who'd since retired, whose forwarding address no longer resolved. He couldn't remember the referral. He ran the contact's name. License lapsed in 2218. Address a service closed in 2220. Social handle a placeholder, gone quiet since 2217. Nothing in the dispute log. Six years ago the man had stopped existing in any system <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could reach.

That happened. People left the work. It usually left more trace than this. There was a difference between missing and gone quiet. Missing was a thing that happened to you. Gone quiet was a choice—and the paperwork here didn't read like accident. It read like maintenance. Every dead end had been kept dead, the way a company dissolves cleanly when it has finished exactly what it was built to do.

He sat with it. Eleven years, and he'd never once asked how he'd come to route his work through an intermediary run by a non-person, owned by a dead LLC with a mailbox that didn't exist, on the word of a referral he couldn't follow—because the man who made it had gone untraceable too. Whatever had been routing his work all this time had done so while leaving no trace of itself. Not careless. Not hidden. Built invisible from the start, and tended that way since.

He'd never asked because the shell had never missed. In the work, that was usually the end of the question.

title: Six Inches
text:
He pulled the shell's transaction log and ran the distribution — categories, districts, intervals. Sixty-three percent of his volume over eleven years had come through the one shell, and he'd never mapped it before. Never had reason to. The work came, he took it or didn't, the money moved. That was the covenant. You didn't audit your broker.

He expected noise. Feast and famine, clusters where a client had multiple needs, dead zones where nothing moved for months. He got clean instead. On every axis the spread sat inside expected variance. No cadence. No center. No clustering. The gaps never ran longer than forty-three days. The neighborhoods rotated through a pattern that kept him moving but never so far he couldn't reach a job in under an hour. Winter, work in the elevated arcologies. Summer, south and east toward the Lake. It looked like someone had drawn it with a compass.

Nothing anomalous.

Which was the tell. Not clean in the sense of tidy — clean in the sense of invisible. A selection built to disappear wouldn't clump. It would space itself across job types, stagger the timing until it read as plain market noise. The variance held inside a band a machine would choose: even pressure, no stress point, nothing that would spike a monitor or draw a second look at the intermediary. Anomalies were what got noticed. The safest pattern was the one so regular it stopped registering as a pattern at all.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ran it again. Same result. He ran it a third time by client signature, by payload type, by risk profile. Same shape every time — the work of someone who understood exactly how detection worked.

He'd run the same play the whole eleven years. Contacts spread thin, work varied, his own signal kept under threshold. Present but never present enough to make friction. He'd done it so long it had stopped feeling like caution and started feeling like weather.

Something turned over low in his gut. He didn't know when the shell had learned to move the way he moved. He didn't know if there'd ever been a version of it that hadn't. Which meant the shell had learned it from him, or it had learned it from something that already knew.

He saved the file. He didn't name it. The screen went dark. The city ran its 0130 shift. The armory sat two floors down.

He looked at the relay.

title: The Log
text:
He opened a new message to the shell.

He typed: *I have a question about the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> job.*

He read it. Deleted it. If the shell was what he was starting to think it was, that wasn't a question. It was a notice — telling the thing he was watching that he'd started to watch back.

He typed: *What is Clearlight Operations LLC?*

Deleted it. The shell would either have no answer, which proved nothing, or an answer he had no way to weigh.

He typed: *Who are you?*

He looked at those three words a long time, his thumb over the send. He deleted them.

The cursor blinked in the empty field. Then he typed one word.

*Received.*

He sent it.

It wasn't a question. It wasn't a probe. It was the word the shell had sent him once — on his closing half-Φ, the first thing it had ever said to him in eleven years. He was handing it back. He didn't know if anything on the other end was there to take it, or whether a thing that had routed his work for eleven years needed him to answer its answer. But it had gone out. He couldn't call it back.

He closed the relay.

title: The Question She Doesn't Ask
text:
He sat at the apartment table for the better part of two hours.

He went through it all again — the carousel notation, the <entity repo="place" guid="019ee6ce-9455-7d19-8916-e2d002eb8e89">Northpoint</entity> variance, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s array reading clean — turning each point over the way <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned a component, looking for the seam where it didn't fit. Nothing changed. The three points sat exactly where he'd laid them out, refusing either to connect or to explain themselves. Somewhere in there he made coffee and let it go cold without drinking it. He stood at the window a while.

At 0247, the relay pinged.

New job. Same shell. Medical transport, short-haul, a loading dock off South Michigan, 0600 contact window — the kind of cover he'd worked a dozen times. Standard rate. Clean scope.

He stood there with the coffee going cold and the job waiting, and at 0247, after two and a half hours of finding nothing wrong with anything, it was very clear to him: eleven years of working with something and never asking what it was had come down to this.

He opened the acceptance field. He confirmed the 0600 window. Then, in the note field — a field he had never once used in eleven years — he typed:

*Query re: Clearlight Operations LLC. Who holds the officer-of-record credential?*

He sent the acceptance.

He sat with the confirmation a moment. The note would route wherever the acceptance did. Something at the other end would receive it. He didn't know if there was a human there to read it, or something else, or nothing at all. But it had gone out. Eleven years, and the first question.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Across the hall</entity>, a bench had six inches of empty space. He'd put it there.

He went to bed. He did not think about the frequency.

title: The Swallow
text:
She had come to the bench to find it — the one name she'd been circling for four days, the reading her own instruments kept refusing to resolve. Today she'd get it or she'd log the failure and stop pretending she could.

She checked herself the way she'd check the array — looking for the thing sitting under the surface, the one she carried and hadn't named. Not fear. She'd run that reading before and gotten the same result twice.

The bench was hers. The stool had been his for four years, and neither of them had ever said so out loud. Her pulse was even, steady in the way hands become when the mind has already decided something and the body is just following through. She wasn't in a hurry. Whatever was in the room could keep, patient as a frequency.

But the marker wouldn't hold still. The moment she locked one reading, the array dragged it half a decimal off and buried the value under a wash of noise that hadn't been there yesterday. She reseated the leads. The drift got worse. She swapped in the calibrated probe she trusted least in the world precisely because it never lied, and it told her the same impossible thing twice, then a third value that contradicted both. The instrument wasn't refusing to resolve the name anymore. It was resolving it into three names, and none of them matched the one she'd come to find. Every attempt to pin it down cost her the last stable number she'd had — the readings weren't just failing, they were unwinding the work behind them.

She noted the tolerance and moved to the next marker.

title: What He Came For
text:
Not the ribs. The ribs were real — the stitched seam, the hairline fracture; she'd felt them both through the tape. But they weren't why <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had come at 2150, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> set in its corner, no word at the door, dropping onto the stool that had never once been his.

He'd come because of whatever that counter in his overlay was measuring. He only opened it when he was carrying something he hadn't named. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had watched him work up to a syllable and lose it. She knew that much of him by now, without being told — the way a tech knows a board is running hot before the numbers say so, from the smell of it, from the set of a face that won't cool down.

And she knew the rest. Three weeks ago she'd copied the carousel cross-streets into the margin of her notes and given him no reason, and he'd asked for none. That was the whole conversation. Neither of them had said a word of it aloud.

The array on her bench was that margin note again, this time built in hardware — the small tidy hand she kept for things she meant to find again. Not the work you do on something broken. The work you do on something you mean to keep reading. Her hands moved through it anyway, checking a connection, seating a lead, the small precise motions that meant she was thinking somewhere behind them.

So she gave herself one thing to get out of him tonight: the name of that counter — what it was tallying, and why it only ran when he sat on her stool. It wasn't in his hardware, or any hardware she could reach; she'd looked. It sat in the overlay like a ghost echo, clearer every time he came in wrong. Say it, or make him.

She kept the calibration running. She didn't close the six inches. She didn't widen them.

title: The Exit
text:
The 17-to-19 Hz band read clean. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> pulled the passive log — eighteen entries since she'd built the instrument, every one flat. No source. No signal in range. Clean meant the city wasn't doing the work for her tonight. Whatever lived at the carousel wasn't here. Maybe it wasn't broadcasting. Maybe a fixed instrument couldn't catch it once it started moving.

She let it go and turned to the motor tendons on Oziel's arm. The prosthetic lay in the vice like a piece of evidence — Nakamura-Brecht, mid-grade industrial, the kind of frame that could outlast its user if the user didn't push it past spec. He'd pushed it. Friday was thirty-six hours out — a real deadline, not one she'd invented to climb down off the edge. Oziel needed the hand to work. That was reason enough to build it right.

The first tendon seated fine. She threaded the second through the wrist channel, drew it taut, and the crimp slipped — the whole line went slack in her fingers. She reseated it. It slipped again. Third try, the crimp held but the tension was wrong, the index finger curling a beat behind the others when she ran the test cycle, a stutter she couldn't dial out no matter how she balanced the load. Every adjustment on one tendon threw another off. The cables wanted to angle inside the sheath, and when they angled the load distribution changed, and when it changed the motors fought each other instead of moving together. The hand kept closing like something half-asleep. She stripped it back to bare frame twice and started the cabling over, and twice the same lag crept back in, and she still didn't know if the fault was the crimp or the channel or something she'd machined a thousandth off true. The kind of problem where fixing one thing broke another until you were chasing your own tail through the sequence.

She knew that kind of problem.

She worked two hours the way you work when the work is the only thing you'll let in the room — not the counter in her overlay she'd been trying not to see, not the stool six inches away that had been empty three weeks now, just her hands and the tendon and the exact millimeter of travel the finger needed. It held. It always did.

title: The Latch Again
text:
The 17-to-19 Hz band stayed flat.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> logged it and moved the probe to the next junction when the relay pinged — that small, specific tone that didn't belong to her terminal, didn't belong to this room. It came through the ferrocement wall like it was announcing itself, like the building itself had decided to speak.

Across the hall.

She set the probe down.

The return ping answered before she'd finished the thought — immediate, no lag. Not a hesitation. Not a question. A relay that had been waiting for that exact message the way a door waits for a key.

She didn't move. She didn't need to. The wall carried it clean: the compression of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s response, the metadata she could almost read if she thought about the shape of it hard enough. She knew the sound of his relay the way she knew the sound of his breath — not because she'd memorized it, but because she'd stopped being surprised by it months ago. The surprise had worn down to simple fact: *he was there, and he was answering, and whatever he was answering to had arrived at 0247 in the morning in a room that was supposed to be dark.*

The third tone came. Addendum. Amendment. Something that changed the shape of what the first message meant.

She picked the probe back up.

Her hands didn't shake. They never did when she was listening. But the crimp on Oziel's tendon suddenly looked loose again, or maybe it had always been loose and she'd only just noticed. She stripped the cabling back, threaded it through the wrist channel again, drew it taut — careful this time, not trusting the hold. She seated the crimp and held it, held it until the tension was right, until the index finger closed in time with the others on the test cycle. Clean. No stutter.

The relay had gone quiet.

It always did, between messages. That was the protocol — the silence that meant someone was reading, deciding, deciding not to answer yet. She'd learned to count that silence the way you count a held breath: one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand, the shape of how long a thought took to become a word.

She made it to eight before the final ping came back.

Not a question. Not a negotiation. Just: *received.*

One word, probably. That was how he did it. That was how you did it when you didn't want the building to hear the shape of what you meant. She knew the feeling. She'd been doing the same thing with the carousel data for four days — logging what she found without naming it, the way you carry something in your pocket without looking at it, the way you know the weight without opening your hand.

The relay went dark.

Across the hall, she heard the latch catch.

Not the door to the stairwell. The door to his apartment. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was moving. Not leaving — the latch had caught from the inside, the way it did when he checked it before bed. The relay had come in at 0247 and he'd answered it and now he was going to sleep on it, and she was going to sit here and finish Oziel's hand and pretend that the ambient noise in her instruments hadn't just spiked at the exact moment the relay had come through.

She checked the motor tendons again. Both seated. Both holding tension.

The 17-to-19 Hz band was still flat.

She pulled the data back and looked at the timestamp on her last entry — 0246, marked clean, marked stable. Forty-three seconds before the relay. Forty-three seconds of the carousel staying quiet, staying dark, staying whatever it was that lived at that frequency when nobody was looking for it.

She reseated the probe and ran the scan again, same interval, same coordinates.

The band spiked.

Not a broadcast. Not a signal from the carousel. A reflection. A harmonic — sharp, clean, source-bearing northeast, his wall, his terminal, the relay opening and closing. Something in the building itself had just woken up and started ringing at the exact frequency she'd been trying to catch for four days, and it had done it the moment he'd answered that relay, and it was still ringing now, still climbing, still refusing to resolve into anything her instruments knew how to name.

She killed the scan.

The room went quiet. Just the ambient hum of the city below, the standard ferrocement background noise. She let it settle. Let the instruments cool. Let the thing she wasn't supposed to be finding go back to whatever it did when she wasn't looking.

Then she opened a new file and started logging the spike anyway — not the reading itself, but the metadata around it. The timestamp, 0247:03, locked. The duration. The frequency band. The correlation with his relay. She labeled it AMBIENT INTERFERENCE — RELAY CORRELATION, just the facts, just the shape of what had happened, the way you write something down not because you're going to do anything with it but because you need to know, later, that it was real.

The file saved.

She closed it.

Across the hall, the building was quiet again. But the silence had changed. It was the kind of quiet that meant something had moved through it — not an absence, but a displacement. The air was still settling. The ferrocement was still remembering the shape of what had just passed.

She picked up the probe and turned back to Oziel's hand.

The tendons were still holding. The index finger still curled clean. Forty-three seconds, and nothing had changed in this room. Nothing visible. Nothing that would show up on a report or a log.

But the bench was hers, and the stool across the hall had just emptied, and the carousel was still broadcasting at a frequency that didn't have a name yet, and somewhere in the overlap between those three facts was the thing she'd come here to find.

She didn't know which one it was.

But she knew how to read it when it stopped hiding.

She ran the scan one more time — the 17-to-19 Hz band, clean, stable, flat as a held breath.

And then she waited to see what the building would do next.

title: After He Goes
text:
The calibration closed out at 0251. She logged it: tolerances in spec, marker three back in range after the humidity adjustment, passive monitor left running overnight. She ran the finger cycle one last time—index through pinky, smooth articulation, no ghost of the crimp that had fought her for two hours. One last look at the band. Seventeen to nineteen, flat, the way it read every night.

She killed the bench light.

In the dark the bench still had its one open span — the width of a man who'd stood there and gone. She left it open. Not out of hope. Not to spite the hope, either. The space was his to cross or not, and she'd settled that with herself a long time back. It stayed open behind her like a held breath, and she let it.

She lifted Oziel's arm into the light of the smaller lamp and found the loose tendon by feel. One more pass before Friday.

But the tendon wouldn't seat. She drew it taut and it held for a second, two, then slipped its channel — the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa79-7c56-942e-c88edc98c6fa">anchor point</entity> had worn oblong, wider than the peg she had to fill it. She tried a shim. The shim fouled the flexor beneath and the wrist locked stiff. She backed it out. Now the wrist had play in the other direction, worse than before she'd touched it. Every correction bought a new fault somewhere down the line, and she was out of Friday and out of the part that would actually fix it, three days from any that could ship.

She kept working.

The Dusk tab softened the room at the edges, and the edges didn't fight it.

They were on the floor of 2E — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s back against the workbench housing, his against the south wall, a gap between them of maybe two feet that shrank and widened depending on what he was paying attention to. She'd put music on, low enough that the rhythm came and went. The light strip sat at the warm end of its range. The workbench was folded up and the cables ran along the shelving with the kind of care that made her apartment feel like a well-kept instrument.

This was the part that cost nothing. They were good at it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was explaining something about a client's array — a modification installed wrong. Not wrong enough to refuse payment. Wrong enough that she'd remember it. She talked with her hands when she was quietly irritated. Her hands were moving.

"He thought he was paying for the premium," she said. "He was paying for the premium. He got standard tolerances in premium housing, and he can't tell the difference, and I have to decide whether to tell him."

"Will you?"

"I haven't decided."

"You already decided."

She looked at him.

"You'd have already told him if you weren't going to," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

She was quiet. Then: "The part that irritates me is that he'll be fine."

"Most of them are."

"That's the irritating part."

The music moved. The light strip ran warm. He wanted this exact thing to last — the low room, the two feet, her hands going quiet — and he set himself to keeping it, to being easy enough that nothing in him tipped it over. He was watching the room without meaning to — the easy, unfocused looking the Dusk allowed — and at some point he noticed he was counting the walls.

He went around. East wall. North wall with its shelving. West wall. South wall with the folded bench. Four. He went around again, slower, tracking where the light sat on each surface. East. North. West.

Between west and south there was a fifth.

Not a wall. Not a shape he could name. A surface, or the hint of one — something in the interval between west and south, in a space where the room had no interval to give. He held still and tried to look straight at it. When he did, the corner was just a corner. West met south at ninety degrees. The seam where the paint had been lapped twice.

He stopped looking.

The fifth thing came back.

He went around one more time, slow. East. North. West. The interval. South. <entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-1757-74fd-8eb3-7e497fc642ab">Five</entity>. Then he looked, and it was four. He sat with that.

"Hey," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

He looked at her.

She was watching the same corner. Her hand was flat on the floor between them, palm down, fingers spread — not reaching, not closing the gap. Checking.

"Same thing," she said. Not a question.

"Yes."

The music had stopped. He hadn't heard it stop.

Neither of them said what the thing was. Neither of them had a word for a corner that held more than the count allowed. He knew what Dusk did — the softening, the deeper colors, the way time stretched in the gaps between things. It did not add walls. It did not sharpen anything. Whatever this was, it was sharp.

Then the pulse came up through the floor.

Low. Below hearing. He felt it in the bones of his seat, in his palms where they pressed the floor — a slow, even vibration at some frequency the body catches before the mind does. One. Two. Three. Four. Then nothing.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> let out a breath.

The room had four walls. The corner was a corner. The light strip ran warm. After a while she started talking again — not right away, not pretending — coming back when she was ready. The client, the array, whether she'd tell him. He answered when she asked him things. It came back: the ordinary room, the floor, the two feet between them. She laughed once at something she said herself.

He stayed another hour. The two feet between them had closed to eight inches at some point, and neither of them had marked it.

When he left she walked him to the door. They stood in the hallway between 2E and 2D a moment — his door was right there, there was no reason to stand in a hallway, and they both stood in it anyway.

He crossed over.

Inside 2D, in the dark, he brought up the array. Everything running. Vitals nominal. The <entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> NeoCortex logged no spike, no surge, no flagged timestamp. Whatever had moved through the room had not moved through his system. Or it had, and left no mark. He held the difference a moment, then let it go.

He didn't know which. He slept.
